Summary:
The CSET issue brief shows how ambiguous, rapidly shifting definitions of “artificial intelligence” (AI) can distort national-level policy analysis of AI competition. Using empirical comparisons, the authors demonstrate that the year in which China, the United States and the European Union appear to “overtake” one another in top-cited AI research changes by up to five years depending on 1) which technical definition of AI is applied and 2) which literature dataset is queried. They propose three expert-informed principles and a SciBERT-based classifier, together with multi-dataset aggregation, as a more stable basis for policymaking.

EXTRACTION CONFIDENCE[87]  
The brief contains clear, linear reasoning from the risk (policy error) through evidence to concrete recommendations, so path extraction is straightforward. Confidence is reduced slightly by the policy rather than engineering focus, which required modest inference when mapping recommendations to the “intervention” schema.

How the instruction set could be improved:
1. Provide an example fabric for a purely policy/measurement paper to illustrate mapping of non-engineering interventions to the lifecycle scale.  
2. Clarify acceptable edge verbs for “addresses” vs “mitigates” to avoid ambiguity when translating narrative logic.  
3. Give explicit guidance for papers where interventions target analysts or institutions, not AI systems.

Inference strategy justification:
All nodes and edges are grounded in explicit statements; only very light inference (confidence 2) was needed to convert narrative recommendations (e.g., “policymakers should…” in “Concluding Recommendation”) into intervention node formats.

Extraction completeness explanation:
Every distinct claim that participates in the causal chain from the identified top-level risk to an actionable recommendation has been captured. Validation evidence nodes encode all quantitative findings (F1 gains, overlap percentages, dataset coverage) that the paper uses to justify its proposals.

Key limitations:
• The brief does not supply numerical uncertainty around metric shifts; consequently, edge confidences rely on qualitative strength descriptions.  
• Interventions are policy-oriented, so lifecycle = 6 “Other” may not merge perfectly with primarily technical datasets.
